Hook: On the fifth of November 2008, Queen Elizabeth opened a new building at the London School of Economics. By then American house prices had been falling for two years, 27 percent from their peak by the time they bottomed, and the rate at which banks lent to each other had just spiked above the Treasury rate: on the tenth of October the gap reached 4.6 points, against about half a point in 2006, the sign of banks that no longer trusted one another. During a briefing on the crisis she asked a simple question. As it was reported, she asked: why did nobody notice it? One of the economists, Luis Garicano, answered that at every stage someone was relying on somebody else, and everyone thought they were doing the right thing.

The question stung. The British Academy gathered economists, officials and bankers to answer it, and in July 2009 two professors, Tim Besley and Peter Hennessy, wrote to the Queen. Their letter concluded that the failure to foresee the timing, extent and severity of the crisis, and to head it off, while it had many causes, was principally a failure of the collective imagination of many bright people, both in Britain and abroad, to understand the risks to the system as a whole. This part reconstructs what there was to see: the theories that predicted this kind of event, the data that warned of it, and how much a careful observer could have known in advance.

This part's question: why do financial systems blow up, and why is it so hard to see it coming? Why does a little bad news, a fall in house prices or one bank's losses, become a collapse of the whole system? What did 2008 look like, in order, from the inside? And can crises be predicted, and what can be done before and after?

Here is the plan. First you judge eight credit booms from history, and meet the old descriptions of how manias end. Then four mechanisms that turn small losses into large ones: falling prices that raise the weight of debt, net worth and the cost of borrowing, collateral, and leverage. The crisis of 2008 in order, and what debt did to households. A hundred and fifty years of data from eighteen countries, to ask whether credit booms predict crises, and your guesses scored. What governments and central banks do in a crisis and before one, crises in emerging markets, and two dials.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: eight credit booms.

Your turn. Here are eight credit booms, chosen by a rule, not by me. From eighteen rich countries since 1955, the eight biggest rises in bank lending relative to GDP over five years, one per country. No crisis happened during any of them, and each economy was still growing in the boom's last year. Your task: decide which of them ended in a systemic banking crisis within the next three years. For scale: in these countries a crisis starts in about 4 percent of peacetime years, so in about 10 percent of all three-year stretches.

Here they are, unlabelled. Each chart shows bank loans as a share of GDP over the ten years to the end of the boom; under it, the rise over the last five years and the change in real house prices. Some are enormous: loans up by seventy points of GDP in five years. Others smaller. Some came with soaring house prices, others not. Which ended in a crisis? Write down your letters. You will see the answers, and how a statistical model fitted only on earlier history would have done, in chapter ten.
Pattern: Chapter two. The pattern: Kindleberger and Minsky.

Start with the historians. In 1978 Charles Kindleberger read centuries of manias and panics, from Dutch tulips to the South Sea Bubble to 1929, and found the same script in most of them. It begins with a displacement: something genuinely new, a technology, a market, the end of a war, that makes some investments more profitable. A boom follows, and it is fed by credit, lending that grows faster than income. Then euphoria: prices rise because they have been rising. Distress: insiders sell, a firm fails, a fraud is found. And revulsion: everyone wants cash at once. It is a pattern read from history, not a model. It does not say when the turn will come, or how far it will go.

Hyman Minsky gave the script its economics. His point was that stability breeds instability: after years without trouble, lenders and borrowers grow bolder. He sorted borrowers into three kinds. Hedge borrowers' cash flow pays both interest and principal. Speculative borrowers can pay the interest but must roll over the principal, so they need lenders to keep lending. Ponzi borrowers cannot pay even the interest, and must borrow more or sell assets, which works only while asset prices rise. The chart is a boom on the Island: four thousand borrowers whose debts grow ten percent a year while their incomes grow two, at an interest rate of three percent. For years almost everyone is a hedge borrower. Then the rate doubles over three years. The same debts, at the new rate, leave only 48 percent as hedge borrowers and make 15 percent Ponzi. Nothing about the borrowers changed in those three years; the boom had built the fragility, and the rate revealed it.
Fisher: Chapter three. Debt deflation, and banks as information.

In 1933, having lost a fortune in the crash, Irving Fisher wrote down the mechanism that had ruined him. Over-indebted borrowers sell assets and cut spending to repay their debts. Prices fall. But debts are fixed in money, so falling prices make each dollar owed heavier. Take a household that repays five percent of its debt every year, while prices fall ten percent a year and real income falls five. Its debt relative to its income rises from one to 1.44 in four years, despite every payment. Fisher's sentence: the more the debtors pay, the more they owe.

That is what happened in America. Between 1929 and 1933 banks' loans outstanding fell 44 percent, as borrowers repaid and defaulted and banks called in what they could. But nominal GDP fell 45 percent, and prices 24. So the weight of the debt that remained did not fall at all: bank loans were 48 percent of GDP in 1929 and 58 percent in 1932. Four years of painful repayment had left the economy as indebted as before.

There was a second mechanism. American banks had always failed in small numbers. From 1930 they failed in waves: 8,812 commercial banks suspended in four years. In 1983 Ben Bernanke argued that this mattered not only because deposits, and so money, vanished. A bank's real asset is what it knows about its borrowers: which farmer pays, which shop is sound. When the bank fails, that knowledge goes with it. Small firms and farmers without a record elsewhere found credit dearer, or found none. He showed that measures of bank failures helped explain the fall in output beyond what the fall in money did. Twenty-five years later, as chairman of the Federal Reserve, he would be in charge of preventing a repeat.
Accelerator: Markets in which borrowers know more than lenders were the subject of Part thirteen. Here is the version that macroeconomics built on. A firm with net worth N wants capital K, so it borrows the difference. What the capital returns depends on luck, omega, which the firm sees and the lender does not. A lender can check, but only at a cost, a share mu of what is left, as in a bankruptcy. Robert Townsend showed in 1979 that the best contract is then ordinary debt: a fixed repayment, and an inspection only when the firm says it cannot pay. Because some firms do fail and checking them is costly, lenders charge a premium over the safe rate, and the premium is larger the more the firm borrows against its own stake. On the Island, with returns that vary as much as small firms' do and a bankruptcy cost of 15 percent, a firm that borrows as much as it owns pays 1.9 percent over the safe rate, and 3.3 percent of such firms default each year.

On the left, the premium against leverage, computed from the optimal contract. It is near zero for a firm that borrows little, and climbs as the firm's own stake shrinks. On the right, a firm deciding how much capital to hold. In green, what capital earns, falling as the firm adds more. In pink, what the firm must pay over the safe rate, given its net worth. It invests where they cross. Now a recession cuts its net worth by ten percent, with nothing else changed: same projects, same safe rate. Every level of capital now means more leverage, so the premium curve shifts up, and investment falls 2.5 percent. In a world without the friction, net worth would not matter at all: this is the Modigliani and Miller benchmark of Part twenty-three. With the friction, a firm's balance sheet is part of the economy's machinery.

Put that inside an economy and it becomes a loop. A loss, say a fall in output or in asset prices, lowers firms' net worth, which raises the premium they pay, which cuts investment and spending, which lowers profits and asset prices further, which lowers net worth again. Ben Bernanke, Mark Gertler and Simon Gilchrist built this into the New Keynesian model of Part thirty, and found that it makes shocks larger and longer-lived. In 2008 the same loop ran through the balance sheets of banks themselves.
Collateral: In 1997 Nobuhiro Kiyotaki and John Moore found a mechanism that needs no information problem at all, only the fact that lenders want security. Farmers are the productive users of land, but they can borrow only against it: no more than what their land will be worth next period. So they put all their net worth into the down payment on land. The land they can hold equals their net worth, divided by the part of the price they must pay themselves, the user cost. The rest of the land is held by gatherers, who use it less well; the user cost is their marginal product, and the price of land is the discounted sum of future user costs. Land is a factor of production and the collateral for the loans that pay for it. That double role is the whole story.

Now an unexpected bad harvest: the farmers' saleable output falls one percent for one period. If the price of land stayed put, farmers would have one percent less to put down, and their landholding would fall 0.67 percent. That is the static effect, and it is small. But the price does not stay put. With less land in farmers' hands, more goes to gatherers, the user cost falls, and so, now and for years ahead, does the price of land. Farmers hold land bought on credit, so a lower price is a capital loss on their whole holding, which cuts their net worth again. Solving for the price and the path together, the fall in the farmers' land is 5.3 times the shock. And it lasts: with less net worth this period, farmers hold less land next period, earn less, and rebuild slowly. The price of land falls by less than one percent, but on a balance sheet leveraged 11 to one that is enough. Output falls 0.74 percent, more than twice the direct loss, and stays low for years as land sits in the wrong hands. Make the shock two percent and, in this calibration, there is no price at which the farmers can keep any land on credit: the model breaks, as balance sheets do in a crisis.
Leverage: Chapter six. Leverage, margins and fire sales.

John Geanakoplos asked what borrowing does to prices when people disagree. An asset pays one if the news is good and point two if it is bad. People differ in how likely they think good news is, from zero to one, and each has one unit of cash and one unit of the asset. The average opinion values it at 0.6. Without borrowing, the optimists buy from the pessimists until their cash runs out, and the price is set by the person at the margin: 0.68. Now let buyers borrow, as much as a lender can lend with no risk, point two per unit, the asset's worst value. Fewer and keener buyers can now own the whole supply, the marginal buyer is more optimistic, and the price rises to 0.75. Leverage does not change anyone's opinion. It changes whose opinion sets the price.

Now let news arrive in two steps. The asset pays one unless the news is bad twice. Today the optimists buy with borrowed money, and lenders, looking one step ahead, lend up to the price after bad news, so buyers put down only 27 percent: leverage of 3.7 to one. Solving for both prices at once, the asset trades at 0.95. Then the first piece of bad news arrives. The optimists who bought on credit lose everything they put down; they were the natural buyers, and they are gone. The asset must be held by the next most optimistic, who are less sure, and lenders, now facing more risk, ask for 71 percent down. The price falls to 0.69, 27 percent. Yet for the person who set the price before, the news lowered the asset's worth by only 9 percent. The rest of the fall is the leverage cycle: the margins and the buyers changed together.

In markets this becomes a spiral. Prices fall; those who bought on credit take losses; lenders, seeing more risk, raise the margins they demand; holders must sell to meet them; and the natural buyers, the specialists who know the asset, are in the same trouble, so the asset goes to outsiders at a discount. Andrei Shleifer and Robert Vishny called these fire sales. Markus Brunnermeier and Lasse Pedersen showed how funding and market liquidity drain together, through the margin spiral and the loss spiral. In 2007 and 2008 the haircuts that repo lenders took on mortgage collateral rose sharply, the run on repo of Part twenty-six.
GFC: In order, then. First, houses. American house prices rose for a decade, faster after 2002, with mortgages offered to borrowers with little income or deposit and teaser rates that reset higher after two years. They peaked in 2006 and fell 27 percent by 2012. As rates reset and prices fell, borrowers who could no longer refinance stopped paying. At commercial banks, the share of mortgages at least a month late went from 1.4 percent in 2005 to 11.5 percent in 2010. This was a large loss, but not, by itself, a large enough one to sink the world's financial system. What turned it into a crisis was where the losses sat.

Second, where the losses sat. Mortgages were made to be sold. They were pooled into securities, and the securities sliced into tranches: the bottom slices absorbed the first losses, so the top slices, rated triple A, looked safe. Banks, and vehicles they set up off their balance sheets, held these securities with very little capital, and funded them with short-term borrowing, overnight repurchase agreements and commercial paper, from lenders who could leave on any day. Long-term assets that were hard to value, funded with money that could run, and no deposit insurance: a bank, built outside the rules for banks, open to the run of Part twenty-six.

Third, the run. On the ninth of August 2007 the French bank BNP Paribas froze three funds, saying it could no longer value their American mortgage securities. Lenders everywhere began to ask what was in each other's books, and the TED spread, the premium banks pay to borrow from each other, jumped. In March 2008 Bear Stearns, unable to roll over its borrowing, was sold to JPMorgan with help from the Federal Reserve. In September the government took over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. On the fifteenth, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, the largest in American history, with six hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars of assets. The next day the Fed rescued the insurer AIG, and a money market fund holding Lehman's paper broke the buck, setting off a run on money funds. The TED spread reached 4.6 points on the tenth of October. Corporate bond spreads went on rising into December. Congress passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program on the third of October. This is what the Queen was asking about.

Fourth, the response. In the fourteen weeks after Lehman, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet went from 0.93 to 2.25 trillion dollars. It lent to banks, to securities dealers, to money market funds, to companies through the commercial paper market, and to foreign central banks short of dollars. Walter Bagehot's lender of last resort, from Part twenty-six, acting for a whole system rather than one bank. How well that worked, and what it cost, is chapter eleven.
History: Chapter nine. A hundred and fifty years, eighteen countries.

Is there a pattern in the numbers, or only in the stories? Moritz Schularick and Alan Taylor, later with Oscar Jorda, assembled bank lending, house prices and the dates of banking crises for eighteen rich countries back to 1870. Here are their data, 88 crises in all. Sort every peacetime year by how much bank lending rose relative to GDP over the three years before, and count how often a crisis started within the next three. In the fifth with the slowest credit growth, 6 percent. In the fifth with the fastest, 18 percent. When house prices were booming as well, 33 percent; when neither was, 5. Robin Greenwood, Samuel Hanson, Andrei Shleifer and Jakob Sorensen found nearly the same in forty-two countries since 1950: about forty percent after booms in credit and asset prices, seven percent otherwise. Crises are not bolts from the blue.

Can that be turned into a forecast? Schularick and Taylor's model predicts a crisis next year from the growth of bank lending in each of the five years before. Fitted on all the data, this curve shows how many crises it catches against how many calm years it raises false alarms in. A useless model lies on the diagonal; the area under the curve is the chance it ranks a crisis year above a calm one. In sample, 0.73. But a forecaster in 1990 did not have the data from after 1990. Refit the model each year on the years before it, and predict the next: since 1950, the area falls to 0.56, barely better than a coin. A simpler measure does better: the rise in lending relative to GDP over five years, out of sample, 0.67. A warning about that number: I tried two measures and am showing you the better one, which flatters it. Credit booms raise the odds of a crisis several times over. But most booms do not end in crises, and the timing is hard.

There is a second regularity, and it is about cost. Take every business-cycle peak in these countries since 1948, and follow real GDP per head for six years. After a normal recession, output dips, and in two years it is back above the peak. After a recession that comes with a banking crisis, it falls further and stays down. Five years on, the normal recession has left output 7.9 percent above its old peak; the financial one, 0.2. The bands show the uncertainty in each average. Over the whole period since 1870 the gap is smaller, about 2 points, and Jorda, Schularick and Taylor found that within each kind, the bigger the credit boom before, the deeper the recession after.
Scored: Here are your eight booms, with their names and what came after. A, Ireland in 2007, B, Spain in 2007, D, Denmark in 2007, F, Sweden in 1990, and H, Switzerland in 1989, ended in banking crises within three years. C, Portugal in 2001, E, Australia in 2007, and G, the Netherlands in 2000, did not, though Portugal and the Netherlands both had crises in 2008, seven and eight years after their booms. Australia, after a boom of forty points, had none. If you marked every one of them a crisis, you were right 5 times in eight. That is the first lesson: the biggest credit booms end in crises far more often than ordinary times do, about six times in ten here against one in ten.

Could a model have done better than you? For each boom, here is the chance of a crisis in the next three years from the simple model of chapter nine, fitted only on the history before that boom ended, ordered from most to least alarmed. It put Ireland and Spain at the top, rightly. It also put Portugal third, wrongly, and Switzerland in 1989, which did have a crisis, at the bottom. Its ranking scores 0.60, where a coin scores one half. That is the second lesson. Credit booms are the best single warning sign we have, but among large booms, telling which will break, and when, is far harder. The Queen's question has a partial answer: the warning signs were there, but signs like them appear in many booms that end quietly, and in the fastest fifth of credit growth, four times in five no crisis follows.
Fighting: Once a panic has started, what stops it? The answers of 2008 are older than they looked. Lend freely, against good collateral, at a penalty rate: Walter Bagehot's rule of 1873, from Part twenty-six, applied to dealers, money funds and the commercial paper market as well as banks. Guarantee the liabilities that are running, as the Treasury did for money funds on the nineteenth of September and governments across Europe did for bank deposits and debt. Put capital into the banks, so that they can absorb losses and lend again: the Troubled Asset Relief Program, first meant to buy bad assets, was used instead in October to buy shares in banks. And find out how big the hole is, and say so. In May 2009 the Federal Reserve published stress tests of the 19 largest banks: 10 needed more capital, 74.6 billion dollars in all, to be raised within six months. Markets had feared worse; once the number was public, banks could raise it. The cost of all this is not only money. Every rescue teaches lenders to expect the next one, which is the case for stopping booms before they start: chapter twelve.

The world's banks borrow in dollars, so a dollar panic is a global one. The Federal Reserve lent dollars to other central banks, which lent them on to their own banks: at the peak, in December 2008, 583 billion dollars. In March 2020, as the pandemic closed economies, the same lines were opened again and reached 449 billion dollars by May. The Fed's balance sheet went from 4.2 to 7.2 trillion dollars in fourteen weeks, and most of the facilities of 2008 were reopened, some within days. The playbook had been written; this time it was run in weeks. Whether its being known in advance makes the next boom bigger is the question that opens the next chapter.
Macropru: If credit booms raise the odds of a crisis, why not lean against them? Rules for a single bank's safety, microprudential rules, miss what happens when all banks lend into the same boom. Macroprudential policy aims at the system. Basel III, agreed after the crisis, added a countercyclical capital buffer: when credit runs ahead of the economy, regulators can require banks to hold up to two and a half percent more capital, to be released in the bust. Many countries also cap mortgages, by the loan's share of the house's value, or by the borrower's debt relative to income. Does it work? Eugenio Cerutti, Stijn Claessens and Luc Laeven studied 119 countries from 2000 to 2013: more use of these tools went with slower credit growth, but much less so in open and advanced economies, where borrowers can turn to foreign lenders, or to lenders the rules do not cover.

Basel's guide for when to raise the buffer is a computable rule. Take credit as a share of GDP, and subtract its trend estimated only from the data available at each date: the credit gap. A gap between two and ten points maps into a buffer between zero and two and a half percent. Here it is for Spain, using bank loans for credit. The gap passed ten points in 1999 and stayed there; by 2007 it was 36 points. The guide would have demanded the full buffer for nine years before the crisis. Spain did have a buffer of its own, dynamic provisions from 2000; Gabriel Jimenez and coauthors found that it cushioned lending in the bust, but it did not stop the boom. For the United States, measured the same way, the guide barely moves, because most American mortgage credit came from securities markets, not bank loans: the boom was outside the measure, as it was outside the rules. The tools exist. Knowing when to use them, and reaching the credit that moves outside banks, is the hard part.
EM: In emerging economies, crises have a signature of their own. In December 1994 Mexico could no longer defend its peso, and within a year it had lost 55 percent of its value against the dollar. On the second of July 1997 Thailand, out of reserves, let the baht float; by January it had lost 54 percent. The panic spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and Korea, whose won lost 48 percent by January 1998. Guillermo Calvo called these sudden stops: foreign capital that had been flowing in for years stops, or reverses, within months, and a country that was borrowing abroad to invest must suddenly cut spending by the whole of the flow.

Why so violent? Barry Eichengreen and Ricardo Hausmann named the reason original sin: most emerging economies cannot borrow abroad in their own currency, so their debts are in dollars. A Thai company owing a million dollars owed 24.5 million baht in June 1997. By January 1998 it owed 53.0 million baht, 2.2 times as much, with revenues still in baht. It is Fisher's debt deflation again, through the exchange rate: the depreciation that ought to help the economy by making exports cheaper bankrupts everyone who borrowed in dollars, and with them the banks that lent. Then the International Monetary Fund lends, with conditions attached. Whether its conditions helped is a long argument, which Part thirty-four takes up with the open economy.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: crises in models and in new places.

Where is the research now? The models of Parts twenty-nine and thirty are usually solved near their steady state, where a crisis can only be a large shock. Markus Brunnermeier and Yuliy Sannikov solved a model with a financial sector globally, and found two regimes. Near normal times the economy is stable. After losses push experts' net worth down, prices, leverage and volatility feed on each other, the loops of chapters four to six, and the economy can stay in the bad region for a long time. And a volatility paradox: when measured risk is low, the experts borrow more, so the system is most fragile when it looks safest. Minsky's idea, as an equation.

Second, the next crisis may not start in a bank. Money market funds, whose shares behave like deposits without being insured, held 3.8 trillion dollars in 2008, when one broke the buck. They now hold 8.4 trillion. In March 2020, in the dash for cash at the start of the pandemic, they had to be rescued again, and even the market for Treasury bonds came under severe strain. Regulators are now asking the questions of this part about investment funds, insurers, private credit and stablecoins, and about risks that are new: a changing climate that reprices whole classes of assets, and a cyber attack that stops payments.

The open questions. When to lean against a boom, and with which tool, given how often booms end quietly. How much of a crisis's cost is the crisis itself, and how much the boom and misallocation that came before it. Whether rescues that everyone now expects make the next boom bigger. Where the leverage has gone, now that so much lending happens outside banks. And the Queen's question, which has not gone away: why the many bright people inside a system find it so hard to see the risk of the whole.
